utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There seem to be no preliminaries. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any technical problem with the earphones of Mr. Mladic, then ... resolved? Yes. It seems to be resolved. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has indicated that the remainder of cross will talk about 45 minutes. I would like to have a discussion with the Chamber and counsel prior to beginning re-examination which actually may shorten re-examination, and I would suggest that if cross-examination takes about 45 minutes that perhaps we could excuse the witness and take that time to deal with that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, seems that you would agree with such way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is all right, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Further, through the VWS, the Chamber was informed that you had forgotten something or left out something in one of your answers yesterday and would like to have an opportunity to complete that answer. You have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was asked -- Mr. Stojanovic asked me yesterday if I had been given any specific taskings relevant to the Mladic case, and I recalled last night that I had been part of large teams in two taskings that were probably relevant. We do large reviews of large numbers of documents for Rule 68, potentially exculpatory documents, and I was involved in that. And also in the initial review of the Mladic diaries, just -- they put together a lot of people who could read Cyrillic handwriting and we just reviewed to see the dates of the diaries, important meetings, and prioritise for translation. I was -- in both cases I was part of large teams. It was not specific to me, but I recalled those as potentially relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for completing that answer. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I hope I am ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you recall, we finished our yesterday's day's work talking about the composition of the Crisis Staffs and participation of the JNA and VRS in individual staffs. Let's try to wrap up this topic. I will put two simple questions to you to that end. Do we agree that, already on the 22nd of May, 1992, the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued a conclusion suggesting that the Crisis Staffs be abolished because as these statement of reasons states, the defence would be taken over by the army? Is that something that you concluded in your report as well?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I base it on the minutes of the government sessions of the 21st and the 23rd of May. The 21st of May doesn't actually specify the abolishment. It leave it is blank. But it says as the army is taking over defence, and on the 23rd they say they have decided to abolished Crisis Staffs. And the day after that, the 24th of May, is when Plavsic issues the instructions on Presidencies. So I think -- I see a logical progression there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you agree - and this is something that you spoke of in your report - that the then-minister of defence in the government of Republika Srpska on 7th of July in an interview for "Glas" magazine also suggested that the Crisis Staffs be abolished; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is quite a leap from the 23rd of May to the 7th of July, but, yes, I certainly cite that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me finish. In your research, did you come across information as to whether any of the municipalities in Republika Srpska following that date - that's to say, post-7 July 1992 - had operational Crisis Staffs still or were they renamed differently, as organs of authority?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some municipalities, they had changed the names from Crisis Staff to War Presidency earlier in June. I believe there are some in July as well. I believe Kotor Varos, but I would have to check the exact dates. But I would note that none of them see -- make a distinction in their operations between being a Crisis Staff and being a War Presidency. They simply regard it as a formal change of name. I know in Kotor Varos they meet in the morning as a Crisis Staff and meet again the same people in the afternoon as a War Presidency. There are certainly some municipalities still calling a Crisis Staff after the 7th of July, but I would have to look more carefully to recall just which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But can we agree that the relationship between the Crisis Staffs and the VRS, with regard to command and control over the army, grew -- growingly different day by day, steadily different, and that it was the VRS that took over the direction of the war?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is what I say in my report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the Crisis Staffs, War Commissions, or War Presidencies, or provisional interim governments, as stated in Zvornik, practically took over the civilian powers of authority. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I say in my report is in the beginning, in the early days, say, in April, they had both powers, or at least a strong role in organising the defence and co-ordinating. They lose that role increasingly as the VRS is formed and takes on that role. But they were certainly, all the time, they were the civilian powers of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move onto a topic which seems to have slipped away in your report, which is the formation of the Crisis Staffs at the level of autonomous regions or districts, as they were called in certain areas. Were you dealing with the powers and the remit of authority of the Crisis Staffs at the level of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I note in my report, there's such an imbalance in the material available. There is so much from the ARK level -- from the ARK Crisis Staff and so little from the other Serbian Autonomous Regions that I'm very reluctant to draw any conclusions. I simply don't know enough. What I do see shows that they did act as an intermediary level. They did assert authority over the municipal Crisis Staffs, and the municipal Crisis Staffs, in turn, cited the Regional Staffs as an authority. But with so much on the ARK and so little on the other regions, I was reluctant to go into any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying then that you in your expert report did not address the powers and relations between local Crisis Staffs and the autonomous region, or Serb Autonomous Districts as they were called, elsewhere in Republika Srpska. Am I right in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mention them only briefly because, as I note, I don't draw conclusions. I do mention them, but I don't have enough material to go into it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I have only one follow-up question where I'd like you to help us with your expertise in that area. The Crisis Staffs at the level of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina, or Autonomous District of Semberija, Majevica, Herzegovina and similar, were they superior to and were there conclusion binding on the municipal staffs? I'm asking you for the period before the 31st of May; that is, before the establishment of the commissions.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is much evidence to that effect, yes, for the ARK. For the other Autonomous Districts there is less, but it is consistent with a hierarchical relationship of republic, then regional, then municipal. But there is so little on the others I'd have to look pretty hard to find the few examples from, I believe, Birac I have a few. But definitely yes for ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us try and place it in a specific situation. You mentioned Birac and you had ample documentation regarding the Bratunac Crisis Staff, so you dealt with that. This is my question: After the commissions were established - that's to say, after the 31st of May, 1992 - who were the Crisis Staffs answerable to under that hierarchy, the Crisis Staff of the SAO Birac, or, if there was one, and we are not sure whether there was one, a Crisis Staff at the level of the SDS or was it the SDS Main Board, or were they answerable to the commissioner appointed pursuant to the decision establishing War Presidencies; in other words, within whose competence did the local Crisis Staffs fall?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Normative documents from the 26th of April, the 24th of May, and the 31st of May all make it clear that Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies were to operate on the directives of the Presidency, the assembly, the government of Republika Srpska, and the Main Staff of the VRS. That would be their ultimate authority. I am certainly not stating that after the 31st of May there was a Crisis Staff at the level of the SDS or the Main Board. The SDS was frozen as a party. There was no more party work at the time. Its leadership had been replaced by that of Presidency. These are now state organs and they are responsible to the highest state levels. As for the Crisis Staff of SAO Birac, I have no documents from them after the 31st of May and indeed we know that the regional authorities were abolished within a few months at the end of the summer of 1992. And I have no reason from the documents I have to think that there was a robust and activity SAO Birac Crisis Staff over the summer of 1992. But perhaps there are documents that were simply never brought to the OTP to show otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at at document in e-court now. It's 65 ter 28394. Your Honours, while we're waiting for the document to appear, let me say that it's one page from the conclusions published in the Official Gazette relative to the conclusions from the meetings of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina for the 15th, 18th and 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, can we look at the conclusion dated the 18th of May, 1992, specifically item 5, which is part of the conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff, and which reads: "Members of other nationalities living in these areas have to defend their centuries' old homesteads under the banner of the Serb republic Bosnia and Herzegovina because peace should be of mutual interest." This is my question: In view of your analysis relative to the Crisis Staffs locally which were part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina namely, Sanski Most, Kljuc and Prijedor, and I would say that you dealt with those the most, this conclusion dated 18 May issued by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was it binding on these local Crisis Staffs in the part where they are called upon to invite members of other ethnicities to join in the defence effort, those who are in the area? So this is my question simply: In formal terms, was it binding?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then let me ask you this: Appreciating your previous answer about the subordination line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, would you please not make introductions of eight to ten lines, explaining all kind of things and then say, in other words, and then phrase a question which has hardly anything to do with the speech you delivered before that. Please, questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is my specific question: Based on your research, would this conclusion issued by the ARK Krajina Crisis Staff reflect the obligations and duties arising from the decisions adopted by the republican level?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I find your question a bit vague. You're saying would this conclusion of the ARK have come from the policies of the republican level. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. The question is under the system that you explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please, rephrase your question. And if you say, Does this arise from the decisions adopted by the republican level, then please be more concrete. If you have one specific decision on your mind, say, Is there any relation with that decision or that decision. But you invite the witness, more or less, to explore a wide area and find a relationship between what you hint at but not specify and this paragraph 5 of these conclusions. So please be very concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the portion dealt with yesterday which relates to the instructions on the formation of the Crisis Staffs dated December 1991. Let me remind you that we spoke yesterday of the Variant A in the first degree, item 11, subparagraph 2, which states in what way the -- the units should be replenished with JNA personnel. So this is, in fact, the context of my question. Would this ARK conclusion be in keeping with the positions expressed in these instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are parallel in that -- well, no. Actually, the A and B is talking about sending Serbs to the JNA. This ARK conclusion is saying that non-Serbs as well should be recruited into the VRS although I would note also in this context numbers 8 and 9 in those conclusions. Excuse me. So in that respect, they're both about getting -- mobilising people into the armed forces with different intentions. But I just think by -- to connect this SDS document of 19 December to the ARK in May 1992 when events had far overtaken A and B is difficult. I don't -- it's hard at this point -- after so much has happened in Bosnia, to -- in those months to connect the two in detail I find difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say, then, that interpreting the conclusion by the ARK Crisis Staff that you're interpreting it as not being in keeping with the instructions issued?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- let me try to see whether I understood the answer well and to see whether we can come to a quick answer to the last question. Do I understand you well that you did not see a direct link between this paragraph 5 and what was stated in the 19th of December, which means no a positive link but also that you do not say it's not in keeping with or -- but that the link is just -- it's so difficult to establish a direct link that you can't either positively or negatively say something about it too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. As far as I know, I see no references in the ARK Crisis Staff documents to Variant A and B to the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not only you do not see any reference but do you see any link in substance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, other than that their Crisis Staffs are organising the defence the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will be done with this document with the following question:

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this position of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on mobilisation which was to include other ethnicities in the defence of the peace, was that, in your view, also the position of the republican organs at the time? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- it was the formal position, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now could you comment, please, Article 9 or conclusion number 9 of this same document, which reads, and this was a conclusion of the Crisis Staff of the AR, that: "Reciprocity should be applied in the moving of the population in the whole territory of the Serb republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." How would you comment this, this position on reciprocity?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conclusion shows that the ARK sees the organisation of the moving out of the population as one of its tasks. They want to apply the principle of reciprocity which I take to mean as many Serbs move into the RS, so many non-Serbs should move out, so it seems to be preparing for the moving out of the non-Serb population. It is not saying we should do everything we can to keep the non-Serbs in the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then, in the context of your last reply, would you please take note of the conclusion of the Crisis Staff of May 20th, 1992, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honour, let me just say that I was unable to find a translation of this conclusion, and I only have the translation of the conclusion of 18th May, and because this is only one sentence, I'll just read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Ms. Hanson, it says in paragraph 1 of this conclusion that there is absolutely no reason for the population to move out from the Autonomous Region of Krajina, no matter what ethnicity. Now could we agree that this is in stark contrast with what you have just said a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it's in contrast with the conclusion 9 up the page. In a -- on the 18th of May, they are saying, We should move out as many Muslims as Serbs come in. The next time they say, There is no reason for anyone to move out. So those two are in contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can the Autonomous Region prevent someone who feels insecure and refuses to accept mobilisation and take part in the war and wish to move out, can they prevent them from it -- from doing so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prevent them from doing what, Mr. Stojanovic? From moving out, or from being fearful, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you then: Can they prevent them from taking this decision to move out for the reasons mentioned above?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if they wanted to they could arrest people and put them in camps but it's -- or forcibly mobilisation them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, can I just understand your question. I don't know -- it is translated: Can they prevent them from taking this decision to move out. Now nobody can prevent anybody from taking a decision. I can take my decision now and keep it to myself and we'll never know that I've decided what I've decided. What actually do you want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps it is an interpretation issue. I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible to prevent such individuals who, for the reasons that I've already mentioned, have decided to leave the area where they had lived previously and to prevent them from moving freely? Would that be possible as all?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, if you have armed forces, you can control the movement of population pretty well. You could also prevent them by reassuring them that they are safe and taking measures to demonstrate their security. Those would be two ways to prevent the movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you use documents, and I will talk about Zvornik specifically, which mention the influx of a large number of Serb refugees into Zvornik. Now, in your report and during your research, did you establish that a large number of Serb refugees had actually come to Podrinje?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may -- those documents that I cite may mention that in addition to the elements of the document that I cite, but I do not recall at the moment any documents which mention it. I'm not saying they don't. It's just not what I was looking at in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, let me ask you this: Did you come across such evidence, and did you assess such documents as exculpatory?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not at the moment aware of such documents, and I don't -- I'd have to see such a document. But on its own, I don't see it as exculpatory regarding crimes against non-Serbs in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please pull up in e-court 65 ter 28413. That's a document that you've used, Ms. Hanson, for your report but in a different context. I would like to refer you to the textual portion of this document, both in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, please, in both versions. Your Honour, there are three documents here that are connected causily. This is a request from Drinatrans, a transport company, addressed to the interim government of the Serb republic -- Serb municipality of Zvornik. They want -- they're requesting payment. This is evidence that it has been paid. And now could we see page 3 of the document which will show us what it was that the interim government made this payment for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, here we can see - could we have the English, please, too? - in this document that you have analysed, Ms. Hanson, we can see that this transport company, Drinatrans, on the 4th of July, 1992, transported along the route mentioned there refugees who were to settle there. And then, again, we see the same thing happened on the 15th of July, the same route, the settlement of refugees. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree it says settlement, "naseljavanje," but they're taking them from Kozluk to the border with Serbia to the bridge on the Drina. And my understanding is Kozluk was a largely Muslim settlement and my interpretation of these documents is removing Muslims from Kozluk and taking them to Gornji Sepak, and I believe their fate was to wind up in northern Serbia on the borders of Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I put to you, Ms. Hanson, that you are completely mistaken, and I put it to you that this is not true and this is why: It is stated clearly here that this transport is along the Zvornik-Kozluk-Gornji Sepak route, and Gornji Sepak would be the end destination, and this is not a place on the border. It is not a town that would imply moving out of people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I am putting a question and I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you differ with the witness just tell her you differ with her, but now you are telling us what your interpretation is which is testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will then finish my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct if I said that Gornji Sepak was not where you implied that it was and what you were referring to had already been dealt with? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a double question. Let's start with the first one. Apparently Mr. Stojanovic challenges that Gornji Sepak is at or close to the border. Is that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to see a map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that answer is there. If there's any way that the parties could agree where Gornji Sepak is, unless there are five or six, but that might resolve certain matters. Now the second part of your question, Mr. Stojanovic, which was, and I have to re-read it, and what you were referring to had already been dealt with. What -- it's not entirely clear to me what that is. But if the witness understands this question, she's invited to answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take him there to be referring to the cleansing of Kozluk, the moving out of the Muslim population of Kozluk. And I believe a large part of the action had already taken place, but it's never as simple as one day the story is over. I would have to review events. But I stand by my assertion that Kozluk was a largely Muslim settlement and non-Serbs removed from Kozluk were crossed into Serbia and wound up, many of them, near the border with Hungary. The exact timing, no, I do not recall. If that had already occurred, then one could read the word, "naseljavanje," the settlement, as bring other refugees into Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This suffices, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honours, and I believe ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were all the questions that I had for this witness, Your Honours. I would to thank the witness. And if you allow me, I would like to tender this document into evidence, because we intend to deal with it further. This is document 28413, 65 ter, and I would also like to tender the Crisis Staff document that I have used, the AP Krajina Crisis Staff, document number 28394.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, first of all, Mr. Stojanovic, I'd like to ask you, you referred to the conclusions of the 20th of May, 1992, for which you had no translation. You read a line from it. Could you please identify the document by its 65 ter number, if it has a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As I mentioned earlier, that's one single document, and it is document 65 ter 28394. That includes the document from which the line was read out. That document includes the conclusions both of the 18th and the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But part of it not translated, if I understand you well? Could we have 28394 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, document 28314 was admitted as Exhibit P57, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was 314 -- or 394; I apologise, if I pronounced not clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you can see the document now in the B/C/S version. And on the following page of the B/C/S version, you can see that these are conclusions of 18 September. They go on to the following page. And then at the bottom you can see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking now at the original. We have -- under number 12 I think we have a decision dated the 18th of May, as we can see on the second page of this document. We have it now. And then we have the next document on this same second page of 65 ter 28394 is a decision or is at least a document dated the 20th of May. What we also see is that that document is not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we understand that you read this part of the document, the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. It's from that same document, document 28394.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then -- so you read paragraph 1 in Cyrillic. Could you please slowly read that one again so that we now at least can follow what you are -- could you read it in your own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anicic, yes. Do you want to tender that [Overlapping speakers] ... if the Chamber would -- if the Chamber would invite you to tender it, would you then do it so as not to make it a Chamber exhibit? Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, this actually highlights one of the issues we wanted to raise regarding the guidance with respect to experts and exhibits. It's a technical matter. If an exhibit has been cited in an expert report, we stand behind tendering all of those documents, and the fact -- simply the fact that it is mentioned in expert report will advise the Chamber means we would tender it, if not for the Chamber's guidance perhaps. So conceptually all of these exhibits are actually Prosecution exhibits; however, given the guidance we're not tendering them affirmatively, and we're recognising the process that they're becoming admitted throughout cross-examinations and throughout the testimony of the experts. As a result, what we're seeing with Ms. Hanson is that many exhibits that are actually Prosecution exhibits are coming in now with D numbers or putting the Chamber in the position of having to make it a Chamber exhibit. What we would recommend or what we would suggest to the Court is that any exhibit that has been mentioned in a Prosecution expert report continue to be maintained or -- certainly we want all of those exhibits in, but that we go ahead and give them a P number regardless of who brings the exhibit in so that we don't have confusion down the road about how what what were originally Prosecution exhibits came before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll consider that. But let's first -- I do see your point. Most important and that may be relevant for the Defence to know, that if you refer to documents which are underlying documents for an expert report that, as the Chamber has suggested a couple of times now already, that if questions are put to a witness in relation to those reports or to an expert witness that those specific documents which have gained the attention of the parties and of the Chamber should be tendered as exhibits. Now whether that should be D exhibits or P exhibits, we'll further consider that, although for the Chamber, exhibits are exhibits, whoever has presented them. So, therefore, Mr. Stojanovic, 65 ter 6408, you said there was no need for you to tender it. But if the Chamber would invite you to tender it, would you do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Yes, I would, Your Honour. I would be prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And if the Prosecution would prefer to make them P exhibits, would you mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wouldn't mind. On the contrary, I accept that. I accept that with pleasure because that document serves -- well, it's really an exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was primarily presented by the Prosecution as underlying material for the -- for the evidence of this witness. Madam Registrar, 65 ter 6408 would receive what P number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P404, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And P404 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next one on my list is 65 ter 28413. It's a bit of a similar story, that it was originally presented as underlying material for Ms. Hanson's report. The Defence has addressed the document. Mr. Stojanovic, would you mind if it would be admitted into evidence as a P Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I wouldn't mind. But if the Prosecution does not seek to do this, then I would be prepared to have it as a D document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Hanson [sic], I understood from your previous observations that the Prosecution -- any document underlying an expert report addressed -- addressed by the Defence that you'd like to have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's accurate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bibles, I should have said. Then, Madam Registrar, 65 ter 28413.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P405, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I'll further discussion with my colleagues whether the way of introducing these documents into evidence, that is, presented as underlying material but not tendered as documents themselves, then addressed by the Defence that that would trigger them to be tendered by the Prosecution, specifically that document in evidence. If there's any document not underlying the report, then they would still become D exhibits if the witness is questioned -- examined on other documents. We'll consider during the break whether what I develop more or less as a system whether that -- whether that obtains the agreement of my colleagues. Then, first of all, Ms. Hanson, we are at a break. We'll start with re-examination after the break. Could you please escort -- could the please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, you wanted to raise a matter. Have we dealt with it? Was it more or less the matter we discussed over the last five to seven minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the first issue. The second issue may be a means by which we can narrow the time required for re-examination, and what I would like to do after the break would be appropriate -- would be to outline those areas where the Defence has challenged Ms. Hanson's opinion where she has addressed that, but we simply need to introduce those documents which -- many of which she has referred to in her testimony already. Where we don't need additional testimony from her, I would like to address those areas with the Chamber, and if we can admit those -- or if we can tender those documents in advance of her testimony, that would reduce the amount of time required to go through those documents or to address them with her on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you propose is that documents addressed during cross-examination which are underlying the report of Ms. Hanson, and where you have no further questions but where you consider it relevant for us to look at those documents, that you list them --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that they are admitted and that no further questions are asked about them. Now, have you given a list of the documents that you would like to deal with in this way to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I have not had a chance to do that, Your Honour. I have just added to the list. I can do that certainly over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long is that list, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I have four categories. My math skills in the courtroom seem to fail me, so I don't want to tender a number but I would say it's less than 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than 50. And they have all been addressed or has the subject matter been addressed?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson's opinion with respect to these particular areas have been challenged, and she has referred in her testimony to many of these documents. For many of these we simply want to go ahead and tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you also carefully look at your list whether there really needs to be 50 or whether there are some core documents which would do. utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've actually just counted, and I unless I have miscounted, I believe there's 18 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 18 documents. That is already a redaction of more than 60 per cent. We'll take a break. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00, then we will let you know whether we can proceed the way you suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like first to address the parties and give some guidance. While -- I'll not give guidance but I'll tell you what the Chamber is inclined to do and then we'll hear from the Defence because we're heard from the Prosecution their position, but we'll then hear from the Defence whether there's any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is inclined to give the following guidance that, as a rule, underlying documents to expert reports used in cross-examination, as a rule, should be tendered but should be tendered as a document of the party that called the expert because it's the underlying material in this case for the Prosecution expert report and, therefore, it triggers an exception to the bar, the bar to tender all of the underlying documents, which we would try to avoid. So, in this case, dealt with by the Defence. Defence will tender it but it will receive a P number. Then, as far as challenges are concerned without the documents specifically used, the Prosecution should have a possibility then to tender documents directly related to the subject matter challenged by the Defence. Now what we would like to hear then from the Prosecution is, first, a specification area of the area challenged, what's the subject matter to which the challenge relates, but very briefly in one or two words, and then that the Prosecution lists the relevant documents it would tender in that context. Now, to the extend if we have already lengthy reports and if cross-examination takes a longer time, then if it would be prepared in writing, that would of course even be better, but if not, for example, for the the 18 documents, just specify the areas - I understand four areas - list the specific documents the Prosecution would like to tender. That is what the Chamber suggests as a way to proceed where we have invited the parties not to tender all the underlying documents. Mr. Stojanovic, any objections to this way of proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber gives guidance to the parties that we should proceed as I just explained to you. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps just to add that, of course, the Chamber always expects the Prosecution to be very selective in what is really needed and what is perhaps related, but not the core of the issue.

utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll receive a bar table motion for those last eight documents. And then, Mr. Stojanovic, we'll receive your response and see whether you'd like to add one or more. utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC

utterances.text: Then P379 is admitted into evidence. May I take it, Mr. Stojanovic, that there was no real re-examination, that it is has not triggered any need to further examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what the Rules say, and I will abide by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that this -- but I'm just looking at my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, this then concludes your testimony in this Court. I would first like to thank you very much for coming to the court. I often add the long way to the court. That might be different in your situation, but we appreciate equally your presence in court and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is always a pleasure to appear before you. May I ask you just to clarify my position now regarding my relations with the Prosecution team, If there's a possibility I could be recalled?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only remaining matter is if there is any dispute about the few remaining documents. Mr. Stojanovic, if there would be any problem, would you be able to inform the Chamber not later than by close of business on this Friday? Or are you already in a position to say that under the present circumstances ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Exceptionally, we are in a very specific situation where the witness is about to leave the court. So, therefore, exceptionally, we allow you to consult with Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic should have his voice at such a level that we couldn't even hear him. He should whisper in your ears, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as soon as we receive the filing, we will respond. I don't think it will require any additional time, save to see if the documents are on the 65 ter list. And I believe that the response will be filed before Friday. As for Ms. Hanson's question, I know what her professional duties are, and we do not mind that she continues her communication. The only thing is should there any need arise for me to put additional questions to you concerning the documents that you used for your report, I will perhaps kindly ask you to return so that I may put these questions to you. I thank you for the work you've done and for the answers you've given on my own behalf and on behalf of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This totally congrues with the opinion of the Chamber, that you are excused and therefore are free to -- to communicate with whomever, perhaps preferably not to discuss in detail your testimony but to do your work and to have the normal communications. That's one. Second, if at any point in time, at the request of the Defence, or if there would be any need to recall you, then, of course, once such a message would reach you - and it is not just the Defence, but the Defence of course would first have to ask leave to re-call, we would decide on that - but if that would ever happen then on from that moment, you are instructed to stop, then, to communicate in the usual way with your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to make clear that the Prosecution will undertake to inform Ms. Hanson about that at the earliest opportunity should that happen, and also to give the undertaking that there is no reason that I can think of that we would need to speak with her about the substance of her report or her testimony, so we will not be doing that in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is appreciated. Then this concludes your testimony. Safe journey home. It's also perhaps a very short journey, but, nevertheless, please come home well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.text: There are a few matters which have to be dealt with before we start with the next witness. And who will take the -- who will examine the next witness, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are drafting the response. My colleague, Branko, deals with the witness, and we will file a written response soon rather than me now giving you a more generalised answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. I do understand that we have a technical problem with a microphone.
